4.  $\text{fp}(t)$: Boundary-to-Interior ($\mathbf{x}_i \in \partial\mathcal{V}, \mathbf{x}_{i+1} \in \mathcal{V}$) [S1].

The claim defines the function fp(t) as 'Boundary-to-Interior' where the starting point x_i is on the boundary (partial derivative of V, denoted as ∂V) and the ending point x_{i+1} is in the interior (V). Source [S1] explicitly discusses the non-reciprocity of the transport kernel due to swapping endpoints changing the case statement, specifically citing 'fp in one case, pf in the other'. In the context of path tracing and the figures referenced (Fig. 4 mentions pp, fp, pf, ff), 'f' typically stands for 'free-flight' or boundary interaction and 'p' for 'particle' or interior medium. Standard notation in this specific literature (likely 'Path Integral Formulation' or similar transport papers) defines 'fp' as a segment starting from a boundary (free-flight source/boundary) to a particle (interior). The evidence states that swapping endpoints changes the case from fp to pf, implying fp is the reverse of pf. If pf is Particle-to-Boundary (or similar), then fp is Boundary-to-Particle (Interior). The notation ∂V represents the boundary and V represents the volume (interior). Thus, the definition in the claim aligns with the logical structure described in the evidence regarding endpoint configurations and reciprocity.
